title: Treaty of Camp Charlotte (1774)
summary: In the October 1774 Treaty of Camp Charlotte, Shawnee leaders under Cornstalk accepted the Ohio River as the boundary, opening Kentucky to settlers.
bodyMarkdown:
In 1774 Virginia and the Shawnee went to war over Kentucky. Surveyors and hunters were crossing the Ohio country and pushing into lands the Shawnee used for hunting, and killings on both sides, including the murder of Mingo leader Logan's family, set the border on fire. Virginia's royal governor, John Murray, the Earl of Dunmore, raised an army. The fighting became known as [Lord Dunmore's War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lord_Dunmore%27s_War).

On October 10, 1774, Shawnee warriors led by [Cornstalk](/people/#cornstalk) attacked the Virginia militia under Andrew Lewis at Point Pleasant, where the Kanawha meets the Ohio. The battle lasted most of the day. Both sides lost heavily, but the Shawnee withdrew across the Ohio.

Dunmore's own column was already marching toward the Shawnee towns on the Scioto. Cornstalk and other leaders met him at Camp Charlotte, his camp on Scippo Creek in present Pickaway County, Ohio. The treaty there, agreed on October 19, closed the war.

By the usual accounts, the Shawnee accepted the Ohio River as their boundary and gave up hunting rights south of it, Kentucky included. They also agreed to return captives and stop attacks on boats on the river. No written copy of the treaty survives, so its exact terms come from later reports, and not every Shawnee town agreed to it.

The quiet that followed opened Kentucky to settlement. In 1775 surveyors and settlers rushed in and stations such as Boonesborough and Harrodsburg took root. The [Transylvania purchase](/stories/richard-henderson/) was a separate, private deal. The Cherokee, not the Shawnee, sold that land to [Richard Henderson](/people/#richard-henderson) at Sycamore Shoals in March 1775, and Virginia later voided it.

The peace did not last. When the Revolution began, British officers in Detroit drew the Shawnee and other nations back into the war, and raids on Kentucky resumed. For Cornstalk's later fate, see [Cornstalk from Point Pleasant to Fort Randolph](/stories/cornstalk-hokoleskwa-point-pleasant-to-fort-randolph/).

## Kentucky today

The treaty was signed in Ohio, but its line shaped Kentucky. A plaque in Pickaway County marks the Camp Charlotte site, and Point Pleasant Battle Monument State Park in West Virginia marks the battle.
